Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I worry obsessively about bad things happening to people I care about
rehearse what to say before any interaction

Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I feel on guard even inside my own home
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.explanation: For a 42-year-old woman whose trauma type is stalking, helicopter or aircraft sounds are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The threat, memory, and maladaptive strategy items all describe hypervigilance, fragmented recall, and interpersonal avoidance consistent with stalking, but no other selected item suggests an aviation-related cue or context. This trigger appears clinically disconnected from the trauma type and from the strong Triggers→Threat / Triggers→Memory pattern in the formulation.

vignette:
Anjali sits in the waiting room, her hands clenched so tightly in her lap that her knuckles are white. She is 42, but feels much older. For the last ten minutes, she has been silently rehearsing the first words she will say to the therapist, trying to arrange the chaos in her mind into a neat, understandable line. It was her husband, Navin, who had finally insisted she come. "I can't watch you live in a cage anymore, Anjali," he had said, his voice gentle but firm. "Not when the door is in your own mind."

The cage had started to form two years ago, its bars forged over six months of escalating fear. It began with Mr. Henderson in apartment 2B. At first, it was just his eyes, how they would linger on her a moment too long in the hallway. Then came the waiting. He would be there when she left for work in the morning and there when she returned, always with the faint, sweet-sickly smell of whiskey on his breath. The terror culminated one evening in the basement laundry room. He had cornered her between the humming machines, grabbing her wrist with a grip that felt like it could shatter bone. A sharp, searing pain shot up her arm. As he leaned in, his face inches from hers, slurring a crude comment, the only thing she could register was the overpowering taste in her own mouth: the cardamom from the chai she'd just finished, now curdled with the metallic tang of pure panic.

Even after the police were called and Mr. Henderson was gone, the feeling of being hunted remained. The memory itself is not a story she can tell; it is a collage of broken shards. A flash of his predatory gaze, the sudden, electric pain in her wrist, and always, that cloying, sickening taste that can rise in her throat without warning. She finds herself pushing the memory away before his words can fully form in her mind, a mental flinching from a blow that has already landed. She cannot construct a coherent narrative of what happened, not even for herself.

Her world has since been remapped according to threat. At home, a place that was once her sanctuary, she feels constantly on guard. Silence is no longer peaceful; when Navin and her son are out, the quiet of the apartment feels like a held breath, amplifying every creak of the floorboards, every groan of the pipes. She is certain that any unusual stillness is a prelude to danger. Before bed, she performs a ritual, checking the deadbolt on the front door three times, then ensuring every window latch is firmly in place.

Her work as a maid has become a landscape of potential ambushes. Last week, cleaning a client's home, she was polishing the dining table when she smelled the stale remnants of wine in a glass left over from a party. The scent was a key, unlocking the memory of Mr. Henderson's boozy breath, and the sour chai taste flooded her mouth. A sharp, phantom pain shot through her wrist, and she had to grip the counter to steady herself. Any man's lingering glance on the bus or in the grocery store feels like a violation, a stripping away of her safety. She has come to believe that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place, especially for the people she loves. She worries obsessively about her son at school or her husband on the road, her mind conjuring vivid, catastrophic scenarios until she is compelled to call them just to hear their voices.

The effort of managing this constant vigilance is exhausting. She rehearses what to say before every simple interaction, from calling a client to reschedule to ordering food, desperate to avoid being caught off guard. Friendships have withered. The thought of sitting in a café, exposed and visible, was too much. She made excuses for months, cancelling plans until the invitations eventually stopped. The isolation is a cold, heavy blanket. Anjali has come to therapy because she is tired of the cage. She is terrified that this fear is all she is now, but she holds onto a fragile hope that one day, she might be able to walk out her own front door and feel nothing but the warmth of the sun.
